description:
We are Space Historians. 

Our team includes Fernando, a developer; Maria Fernanda and Maysa, who are students; and Sabrina, a marketing and content strategist who loves philosophy and neuroscience. We all share a passion for rock music, AI, and great stories. 

Together, we want to revive the stories of forgotten space explorers using creative storytelling and technology. 

We believe that every mission has a story to tell, and every discovery can inspire the next generation.
summary:
Space Historians is a 3D web game for kids aged 8 to 12. It's a game which takes them to the Moon and allows them to explore the equipment and spacecraft components that have been left behind by the various lunar missions.

Players become astronauts and follow a route linking 12 discoveries. At each stop they unlock an interactive card containing the mission details, the science, the history and activities.

The project presents lunar legacy in a format children can explore for themselves. Instead of reading mission information in an article or database, they learn by finding each object, examining it and gradually uncovering its story.

The current prototype includes a navigable 3D lunar environment, 12 discoveries, Portuguese and English interfaces, keyboard and touchscreen controls, interactive activities, and a points system. Progress is saved locally in the browser.

The game runs online so there's nothing to install. It gives kids a very accessible introduction to space science, space engineering and space history and also shows them why the things we've left on the Moon are worth studying and worth preserving.
details:
Space Historians is a browser-based educational 3D exploration game for children aged 8 to 12.

Players control an astronaut, explore a very small scale model of the Moon and investigate 12 scientific instruments, vehicles and spacecraft elements from the Apollo missions and Surveyor 3.

The project was designed to turn the history of space and scientific data into an active learning experience. Rather than just get points for moving around the environment, you get points for learning.

Each discovery contains three progressive learning layers: identifying the object, understanding how it worked and why it mattered, and exploring its historical and human context. Completing these layers awards points and records the discovery. Optional quizzes provide bonus points, reinforcing learning without preventing players from continuing the exploration.

The 12 discoveries are: the Apollo 12 ALSEP station, Surveyor 3, the Apollo 14 ALSEP, the Apollo 15 ALSEP and Lunar Rover, the Apollo 16 ALSEP and Lunar Rover, the Apollo 11 laser reflector, the Eagle descent stage, the Apollo 11 passive seismometer, the Apollo 17 ALSEP and the Apollo 17 Lunar Rover.

Players navigate with WASD, arrow keys, or a touchscreen joystick and investigate objects through proximity-based interactions. Discovery cards present mission information, real NASA photographs where available, interactive activities, simplified educational simulations, and sections distinguishing documented facts from narrative adaptation. Progress is stored locally in the browser so players can continue their learning journey.

Space Historians benefits young learners by connecting science, engineering, history, and human stories through play. It aims to spark curiosity about space exploration, make technical knowledge easier to understand, and invite children to see the Moon as humanity’s first museum beyond Earth, where every object holds a story of ingenuity, discovery, and courage.

The prototype was developed as a web experience using TypeScript, Vite, Babylon.js, WebGL, HTML, and CSS. It includes an official NASA Apollo Lunar Module 3D model, an attributed astronaut model by Poly by Google, CC0 environment assets from Kenney, and simplified 3D representations created for accessibility and browser performance.

The content system separates stories, translations, images, activities, scoring, and object data from the 3D environment, allowing the project to grow without rebuilding its core architecture.

Our creative process began with research into Apollo landing sites, mission equipment, scientific experiments, and objects that remain on the Moon. We organized these discoveries into an educational route, designed a child-friendly narrative, and iteratively tested navigation, interaction, readability, scoring, and browser performance.

OpenAI ChatGPT and Codex, as well as Anthropic Claude, supported coding, debugging, documentation, content organization, translation preparation, and testing. The team remained responsible for research, writing the stories, source verification, educational decisions, design direction, testing, and final implementation.

The team considered accessibility for children, mobile and desktop compatibility, performance on ordinary web browsers, transparent source attribution, bilingual access, and a modular structure that can support new content. The current experience is available in Portuguese and English.

In the next phase, we plan to add Spanish as a third complete language and expand the same educational model beyond the Moon to Mars. A future Mars expedition could introduce robotic missions, rovers, landers, scientific instruments, and evidence gathered through planetary exploration.

Space Historians brings science, engineering, and history together in a format children can explore for themselves. We want to make space research easier to understand and show that the objects left on the Moon are not just old equipment.

Each one can tell us something about how people explored, worked, solved problems, and learned in an unfamiliar place.
